props.title: Things You Can Tell Just by Looking at Her
props.initialSlug: Five women's lives intertwine in LA love stories

sections.content: Things You Can Tell Just by Looking at Her represents a masterful exploration of interconnected female narratives, similar to Robert Altman's Short Cuts (1993) but with a more intimate focus. Director Rodrigo García weaves together five vignettes featuring women in Los Angeles, each grappling with love, loneliness, and identity. The film's power lies in its subtle observations and outstanding ensemble cast including Glenn Close, Holly Hunter, and Cameron Diaz. It shares DNA with later works like Nine Lives (2005) and Mother and Child (2009), both also directed by García, in its nuanced portrayal of women's interior lives.

sections.content: The film marked a crucial moment in independent cinema's treatment of women's stories. Unlike the glossier Erin Brockovich (2000) or Charlie's Angels (2000) released the same year, García's approach favors quiet moments and unspoken emotions. The influence of this storytelling style can be seen in later works like Crash (2004) and The Hours (2002), though García's touch remains more delicate and observational. SUBHEAD: The Evolution of Multi-Narrative Women's Stories

García's influence extends to contemporary filmmakers exploring female-centered ensemble narratives. Certain Women (2016) follows a similar template of interconnected stories in a specific location, while 20th Century Women (2016) shares its interest in complex female relationships across generations. The legacy of Things You Can Tell can also be seen in television, particularly in series like In Treatment, which García would later direct, showing his continued interest in intimate character studies.
